person.name: Friedensreich_Hundertwasser
person.summary: Friedensreich Hundertwasser was an Austrian painter, architect, and environmentalist who rejected straight lines and standardized building. His colorful works joined irregular forms with vegetation, and he promoted trees, roof gardens, and individual expression in cities.

conclusion: Friedensreich Hundertwasser’s paintings, prints, and graphic designs remain in museum collections and exhibitions around the world. The Hundertwasser House continues to serve as housing in Vienna. His architectural designs were realized in Austria, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, and the United States.

events.title: Birth in Vienna
events.description: Friedrich Stowasser was born in Vienna as the only child of engineer Ernst Stowasser and Elsa Stowasser, née Scheuer. His parents' families came from Bohemia and Moravia, respectively.

events.title: Loses His Father
events.description: In 1929, Ernst Stowasser died in Vienna of appendicitis shortly after Friedrich’s first birthday. Elsa Stowasser raised Friedrich as her only child.

events.title: Survives Nazi Rule
events.description: After Austria’s annexation by Nazi Germany in 1938, Elsa Stowasser moved Friedrich from a private school to a state school in Vienna. Private-school pupils drew attention. Nazi authorities forcibly moved Elsa and Friedrich to housing in Vienna’s Leopoldstadt district. They survived Nazi persecution. Friedrich’s maternal grandmother and about 70 other relatives were killed.

images.caption: Austrian Nazi propaganda from the 1938 Anschluss
images.creator: Thomas Quine

events.background:
Elsa Stowasser’s Jewish background placed the household in danger under Nazi rule. The article connects Friedrich’s experience of persecution to the anti-totalitarian position he held from an early age.

He later linked geometric order with political coercion. The article says that fears of battalions marching in square formations during 1938–45 may have contributed to his rejection of the geometric ordering of people and buildings. In a 1954 letter, he described rectangles as marching columns pressed into geometric formations.

events.title: Leaves the Vienna Art Academy
events.description: Friedrich Stowasser completed his Matura at Bundesgymnasium Horn in 1948. He enrolled at the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna for the 1948–49 winter semester. He left after three months and began signing his works Hundertwasser.

Matura.explanation: Matura is the Austrian secondary-school leaving examination that qualifies students for higher education.

events.title: Meets René Brô in Italy
events.description: In April 1949, Hundertwasser made his first journey to Italy and met the French artist René Brô. He carried a miniature paintbox on the journey. In 1950, the two artists traveled together toward Paris.

events.title: Forms Transautomatism
events.description: In Paris, Hundertwasser joined debates among artists and critics over geometric and expressive abstraction. He encountered [[Informel]], a postwar European approach to abstract art, and [[Tachism]], a style of spontaneous, chance-led painting. He formulated [[Transautomatism]], which asks viewers to take an active and responsible part in perceiving and shaping an artwork. His Paris contacts included Michel Tapié, Yves Klein, Pierre Restany, and Julien Alvard.

Transautomatism.explanation: Hundertwasser used this name for his own response to postwar abstract painting. It placed responsibility for completing the artistic experience partly with the viewer.

Tachism.explanation: The name comes from the French word tache, meaning stain or spot. Critics used it for a branch of Art Informel associated with spontaneous marks.

Informel.explanation: Often called Art Informel, this European postwar movement favored unplanned, gestural forms over geometric order.

events.title: Draws an Uninterrupted Classroom Line
events.description: In December 1959, visiting lecturer Friedensreich Hundertwasser joined Bazon Brock, Herbert Schuldt, and students at the Hamburg University of Fine Arts. They drew the Unendliche Linie, an uninterrupted line through a classroom. The school director stopped the action, and Hundertwasser resigned his teaching post.

events.title: Wins the Mainichi Prize in Tokyo
events.description: In 1961, Hundertwasser traveled to Tokyo for the Sixth International Art Exhibition and received the Mainichi Prize. In Japan, he rendered his first name in Japanese characters for peace and wealth as he developed the artistic name Friedensreich.

events.title: Shows at the Venice Biennale
events.description: In 1962, the Austrian Pavilion at the Venice Biennale presented a retrospective of Friedensreich Hundertwasser’s work in Venice. The Venice Biennale is an international exhibition of contemporary art. Vinzenz Oberhammer organized the retrospective.

events.title: Makes a Home in Waldviertel
events.description: In 1966, Hundertwasser bought the disused Hahnsäge sawmill in the Waldviertel region of Lower Austria. He converted the property into a home and lived there amid the surrounding forest.

events.title: Restores Kaurinui Valley
events.description: After a touring exhibition in New Zealand and Australia, Hundertwasser acquired several properties in Kaurinui Valley in the Bay of Islands. He planted more than 100,000 native trees there. He built ponds, canals, and natural wastewater systems on the land.
events.background:
The holdings covered about 372 hectares and encompassed the whole Kaurinui Valley. Hundertwasser treated the land as a project of returning territory to nature and giving nature its rights.

Solar collectors and a waterwheel supplied energy on the property. He used a composting toilet there. An old farmhouse provided living and working space. He also used his designed Bottlehouse, the Pigsty, and the Mountain Hut for those purposes.

events.title: Publishes the Tree Tenant Manifesto
events.description: At the Milan Triennale, an international design exhibition, Hundertwasser placed about 15 trees through windows along Via Manzoni. He published Inquilino Albero, an essay that called trees tenants of the buildings that contain them.

events.title: Designs Rosenthal’s Factory Facade in Selb
events.description: In 1982, Friedensreich Hundertwasser designed the facade of the Rosenthal porcelain factory in Selb, West Germany. He brought irregular forms and vivid colors to the industrial building.

events.title: Defends Hainburg Wetlands
events.description: In 1984, Friedensreich Hundertwasser joined activists occupying the Hainburger Au near Hainburg to oppose a planned Danube power plant. At a press conference in Vienna, he tore up the Great Austrian State Prize, a state cultural award he had received.

events.title: Hundertwasser House Opens in Vienna
events.description: On February 17, 1986, the City of Vienna handed the Hundertwasser House over to its tenants. Friedensreich Hundertwasser devised the building’s artistic concept. Josef Krawina prepared its initial planning, and Peter Pelikan continued the architectural work. The building has irregular floors, planted terraces, a brightly colored facade, and trees.
events.background:
The house was built between 1983 and 1985 after the City of Vienna had commissioned Josef Krawina in the late 1970s to plan municipal housing from Hundertwasser’s ideas. Peter Pelikan joined its planning in 1981. The project became Hundertwasser’s first practical architectural work after years of architectural manifestos and model designs.

The completed building immediately became a tourist attraction. The wider public generally responded favorably to Hundertwasser’s architectural projects. Architects and professional critics often opposed them sharply.

events.title: Dies at Sea
events.description: On February 19, 2000, Hundertwasser was returning from New Zealand to Europe aboard the passenger ship Queen Elizabeth 2. He died of heart failure at sea off Brisbane, Australia.
